title: Learning to Ask for Help
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article argues that leaders' resistance to asking for help is rooted in a self-imposed misconception — that needing help reads as weakness — when in practice colleagues would gladly assist and wouldn't judge the requester as incompetent. The author uses a role-reversal thought experiment to expose the inconsistency in this belief, then recommends treating help-seeking as a muscle to be strengthened through small, low-stakes requests before it's genuinely needed. The piece frames this as essential for leaders' own productivity and growth, not just team performance.
points: Leaders often treat asking for help as a weakness, even though they would never judge a team member harshly for asking them the same thing.
The role-reversal thought experiment — would you think less of a team member for asking you for help? — exposes the double standard leaders apply to themselves.
Asking for help is described as a muscle that gets easier with practice, best built through small, low-stakes requests before a real crisis arrives.
No one achieves extraordinary long-term outcomes without substantial help from others along the way.
quotes: One of the most difficult things for many leaders to learn is how to ask for help when they need it.
Too often, asking for help is viewed as a weakness or a surrender rather than a strength.
A leader who admits they don’t know how to do something or can’t get something done without some assistance doesn’t display weakness.
No one achieves long-term success without the help of a small army of people who listen, share advice, lend a hand, push and challenge, and advocate for them.
Get in the habit of asking for help when it isn’t critical and you’ll have an easier time finding the courage to request a hand when you need it most.
